questions.question: A village that regularly suffers from drought wants to store water for dry seasons to irrigate the agricultural field. Which method will help most?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Rainwater harvesting and watershed management**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Rainwater harvesting** is the process of collecting, filtering, and storing **rainwater** from surfaces like rooftops or open ground for future use. This technique is the most effective way for a drought-prone village to ensure water availability during **dry seasons**.
 
• **Watershed management** refers to the efficient management and conservation of surface and **groundwater** resources. It involves techniques like **contour bunding**, **trenching**, and the construction of **check dams** to prevent soil erosion and increase water percolation into the soil.
 
• The primary goal of these methods is to **recharge groundwater** tables and create surface storage, such as **farm ponds** or **percolation tanks**, which can be directly used for **irrigation**.
 
• By implementing **watershed management**, a village can transform its hydrological cycle, ensuring that even with low rainfall, the moisture levels in the **agricultural field** are maintained.
 
• These methods are sustainable and cost-effective, often involving local communities in the **planning** and **maintenance** of water structures, leading to long-term **water security**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Sprinkler Irrigation:** This is a method of applying **irrigation** water which is similar to natural rainfall. While it improves **water-use efficiency**, it does not solve the problem of *storing* water for dry seasons; it only helps in using existing water more carefully.
 
• **Growing short-duration crops:** This is a **drought-escape** strategy. Crops like **millets**, **pulses**, or **oilseeds** that mature in **60 to 90 days** are grown to avoid the peak dry period. However, this does not provide a storage solution for water.
 
• **Spraying pesticides:** This practice is used to protect crops from **pests and diseases**. It has no relevance to water conservation or **drought mitigation**.
 
• **Government Initiatives:** The **Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana (PMKSY)**, launched in **2015**, focuses on **'Per Drop More Crop'** and **'Har Khet Ko Pani'** by promoting **watershed development** and **micro-irrigation**.
 
• **Catch the Rain Campaign:** Launched by the **Ministry of Jal Shakti** in **2021**, this campaign encourages states and stakeholders to create appropriate **Rain Water Harvesting Structures (RWHS)** suitable to the climatic conditions before the onset of **monsoon**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Groundwater Depletion:** According to reports, India is the largest user of **groundwater** in the world. Techniques like **rainwater harvesting** are critical because the **Central Ground Water Board (CGWB)** has identified several areas as "over-exploited."
 
• **Traditional Methods:** Many regions in India use traditional storage systems such as **Johads** in **Rajasthan**, **Zabo** in **Nagaland**, and **Eris** in **Tamil Nadu**, which are excellent examples of **watershed management**.
 
• **Economic Impact:** Proper **water management** can increase crop intensity and diversify **agriculture**, allowing farmers to grow a second crop in the **Rabi season** (winter), significantly boosting **rural income**.
 
• **Environmental Benefits:** Beyond **irrigation**, these practices help in restoring the **ecosystem**, reducing **soil salinity**, and supporting local **biodiversity**.

questions.question: What is required to describe the distance an object has travelled?

options.text: The starting and ending points only
Only the numerical value, which is its magnitude

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Only the numerical value, which is its magnitude**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Distance** is defined as the total path length covered by an object during its motion from one point to another. It describes how much ground an object has covered regardless of its starting or ending position.
 
• To describe distance, we only need the **numerical value**, which is known as its **magnitude**. It does not require any information about the **direction** of motion. ***Hence, option D is the correct statement.***
 
• Option A suggests both **magnitude** and **direction** are required; however, this describes **displacement**, which is a vector quantity, not distance. ***Hence, statement A is incorrect.***
 
• Option B mentions the **starting and ending points** only; while these define the **displacement** (the shortest straight-line path), they do not account for the actual path taken to determine distance. ***Hence, statement B is incorrect.***
 
• Option C states only the **direction of motion** is needed; direction alone cannot quantify the extent of travel without a **numerical value**. ***Hence, statement C is incorrect.***
 
• The **SI unit** of distance is the **meter** (m), as established by the **International System of Units**. Other common units include **kilometers** (km), **centimeters** (cm), and **miles**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Scalar Quantities:** These are physical quantities that are described by **magnitude** only. Examples include **distance**, **speed**, **mass**, **temperature**, **time**, and **energy**. They follow ordinary algebraic laws for addition and subtraction.
 
• **Vector Quantities:** These require both **magnitude** and **direction** for a complete description. Examples include **displacement**, **velocity**, **acceleration**, **force**, and **momentum**. These quantities follow **vector algebra** rules.
 
• **Speed vs. Velocity:** **Speed** is the rate of change of **distance** (scalar), whereas **velocity** is the rate of change of **displacement** (vector). A car moving at **60 km/h** describes speed, but a car moving at **60 km/h towards the North** describes velocity.
 
• **Path Dependency:** Distance is **path-dependent**, meaning if a person walks **4 meters** North and **3 meters** East, the total **distance** traveled is **7 meters**. However, the **displacement** (magnitude) would be **5 meters** (calculated using the **Pythagoras theorem**).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Odometer:** This is a **device** or **instrument** installed in **vehicles** (like cars and bikes) to measure the total **distance** traveled by the vehicle. It records the **numerical value** in **kilometers** or **miles**.
 
• **Positivity:** The **distance** traveled by a moving object can **never be zero** or **negative**. It is always a **positive** quantity as long as the object is in motion. In contrast, **displacement** can be **zero** if the object returns to its **initial position**.
 
• **Relationship:** For motion in a **straight line** without changing direction, the **magnitude** of **distance** is equal to the **magnitude** of **displacement**. In all other cases involving curves or turns, **distance** is always **greater** than the magnitude of **displacement**.
 
• **Calculation:** Distance can be calculated using the formula **Distance = Speed × Time**, provided the speed is constant over the given **time** interval.

questions.question: Which property of a carbon atom enables one carbon atom to form bonds with other carbon atoms?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Catenation**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Catenation** is the unique property of **carbon atoms** to form **covalent bonds** with other **carbon atoms**, resulting in the formation of long **chains**, **branched chains**, or **closed rings**. This ability is the primary reason for the vast number of **organic compounds** existing in nature.
 
• The strength of the **carbon-carbon (C-C) bond** is exceptionally high (approximately **348 kJ/mol**), which makes the resulting structures very stable. While other elements like **Silicon** or **Sulphur** show catenation, their bond strengths are much lower, limiting the length of their chains.
 
• Carbon exhibits **maximum catenation** due to its **small atomic size** and the high strength of the bond formed between its atoms. This allows carbon to link in various configurations, including **straight chains**, **branched structures**, and **cyclic rings**. *Hence, the statement regarding catenation is correct.*
 
• This property enables carbon to form **millions of compounds**, which are studied under a dedicated branch of science known as **Organic Chemistry**. The compounds can range from simple molecules like **Methane (CH4)** to complex biological molecules like **DNA** and **Proteins**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Tetravalency:**

 
 
• Carbon has an **atomic number** of **6**, with an electronic configuration of **2, 4**. It has **four valence electrons** in its outermost shell.
 
• To achieve stability, it forms **four covalent bonds** with other atoms. This **tetravalency** allows carbon to bond with oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen, and halogens, leading to a diverse range of **functional groups**.
 
 
 
• **Polymerisation:**
 
 
• This is a process where small units called **monomers** combine chemically to form a large, three-dimensional network or chain called a **polymer**.
 
• Common examples include **Polyethylene** (formed from ethylene monomers) and **PVC**. While carbon compounds undergo polymerisation, the fundamental property that allows carbon to link with itself in the first place is **catenation**. *Hence, this option is related but not the fundamental property asked.*
 
 
 
• **Isomerisation:**
 
 
• **Isomerism** is the phenomenon where compounds have the same **molecular formula** but different **structural arrangements** or spatial orientations.
 
• **Isomerisation** is the chemical process by which one molecule is transformed into another molecule which has exactly the same atoms, but the atoms are rearranged. This contributes to the diversity of carbon compounds. *Hence, this option describes a structural variation rather than the bonding ability itself.*
 
 
 
• **Allotropes of Carbon:**
 
 
• Carbon exists in several **allotropic forms** such as **Diamond**, **Graphite**, and **Fullerenes** (like **C60**).
 
• In **Diamond**, each carbon atom is bonded to **four** others in a **tetrahedral** structure, while in **Graphite**, carbon atoms form **hexagonal layers**. These structures are possible due to the **catenation** property.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Bonding Versatility:** Carbon can form **single** (alkanes), **double** (alkenes), and **triple** (alkynes) bonds. The **bond length** decreases as the number of bonds between two carbon atoms increases, with **triple bonds** being the shortest and strongest.
 
• **Comparison with Silicon:** Silicon belongs to the same group (**Group 14**) as carbon and shows catenation. However, due to its larger **atomic size**, the **Si-Si bond** is weaker, and it usually forms chains only up to **7 or 8 atoms**, unlike carbon which can form chains of **thousands of atoms**.
 
• **History and Discovery:** The study of carbon-based compounds dates back centuries, but the term **Organic Chemistry** was popularized in the **19th century**. The synthesis of **Urea** by **Friedrich Wöhler** in **1828** disproved the "Vital Force Theory," showing that carbon compounds could be created from inorganic materials.

questions.question: What is the range of the pH scale?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**0 to 14**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **pH scale** is a tool used to specify the **acidity** or **basicity** (alkalinity) of an aqueous solution. It was first introduced by the **Danish** biochemist **Soren Peder Lauritz Sorensen** in the year **1909**.
 
• The standard range of the pH scale is from **0 to 14**. This range allows for the classification of substances based on their **hydrogen ion** concentration. ***Hence, Option A is correct.***
 
• A **pH** value of **7** is considered **neutral**, which is the characteristic of **pure water** at **25 degrees Celsius**. It represents a balance between **hydrogen ions** (H+) and **hydroxyl ions** (OH-).
 
• Substances with a **pH** value less than **7** (specifically from **0** up to **7**) are classified as **acidic**. The lower the **numerical value**, the stronger the acid. ***Hence, Option B is incorrect as it only represents the acidic portion of the scale.***
 
• Substances with a **pH** value greater than **7** (specifically from **7** to **14**) are classified as **basic** or **alkaline**. The higher the **number**, the stronger the base. ***Hence, Option D is incorrect.***
 
• While **pH** values can occasionally fall outside the **0 to 14** range for extremely strong chemicals, the standard operational scale used in laboratories and for educational purposes is **0 to 14**. ***Hence, Option C is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Logarithmic Nature:** The **pH scale** is **logarithmic**, meaning each whole **pH** value below **7** is **10 times** more **acidic** than the next higher value. For example, **pH 4** is **ten times** more acidic than **pH 5** and **100 times** (10 times 10) more acidic than **pH 6**.
 
• **Biological Importance:** The **pH** level is critical in biological systems. For instance, the **pH** of **human blood** is tightly regulated between **7.35 and 7.45**. Any significant deviation can lead to serious health issues or death.
 
• **Examples of Acidic Substances:** Common **acidic** substances include **gastric juice** (pH **1.5 to 3.5**), **lemon juice** (pH **2.0**), **vinegar** (pH **2.9**), and **coffee** (pH **5.0**).
 
• **Examples of Basic Substances:** Common **alkaline** substances include **baking soda** (pH **9.0**), **milk of magnesia** (pH **10.5**), and **household bleach** (pH **12.5**).
 
• **Measurement Tools:** The **pH** of a solution can be measured using **pH paper**, **Universal Indicator**, or electronic **pH meters**. **Litmus paper** is a basic tool that turns **red** in acids and **blue** in bases.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Temperature Dependence:** The **pH** of a solution is dependent on **temperature**. The **neutral point** of **7** is only strictly accurate at **25 degrees Celsius** (**298 Kelvin**). As temperature increases, the **neutral pH** value slightly decreases.
 
• **pOH Concept:** Parallel to **pH**, there is a **pOH** scale which measures the concentration of **hydroxide ions**. In any aqueous solution at **25 degrees Celsius**, the sum of **pH** and **pOH** always equals **14**.
 
• **Environmental Impact:** The **pH** of **rainwater** is typically around **5.6** due to dissolved **carbon dioxide**. However, **acid rain** occurs when the **pH** drops below **5.6**, often caused by **sulfur dioxide** and **nitrogen oxides** emitted from industrial processes.
 
• **Chemical Definition:** Mathematically, **pH** is defined as the **negative logarithm** (base **10**) of the **hydrogen ion** activity: **pH = -log10[H+]**.

questions.question: What is 'suspension' in chemistry?

options.text: A heterogeneous mixture with large particles

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**A heterogeneous mixture with large particles**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **suspension** is a **heterogeneous mixture** in which the **solute**-like particles settle out of a **solvent**-like phase some time after their introduction. *Hence, statement A is correct.*
 
• The **particle size** in a **suspension** is quite large, typically greater than **1000 nanometers** (or **1 micrometer**), which allows them to be seen clearly with the **naked eye**.
 
• Unlike **homogeneous mixtures**, where the components are distributed uniformly at a molecular level, the components of a **suspension** are **non-uniformly distributed**. *Hence, statement B is incorrect.*
 
• A **suspension** is considered **unstable** because the particles will eventually **precipitate** or **settle down** at the bottom of the container due to the influence of **gravity** if left undisturbed for a **period of time**.
 
• The large **particle size** prevents **suspensions** from passing through **filter paper**, meaning they can be easily separated by **physical methods** such as **filtration** or **decantation**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Tyndall Effect**: A **suspension** scatters a beam of light passing through it, making its path **visible**. This phenomenon is known as the **Tyndall Effect**. However, if the particles **settle down** completely, the mixture may lose this property.
 
• **Comparison with Solutions**: A **true solution** is a **homogeneous mixture** where the **solute particles** are less than **1 nanometer** in diameter and do not scatter light or settle. *Hence, statement C is incorrect.*
 
• **Colloidal Dispersions**: A **colloid** is a **heterogeneous mixture** where the **particle size** is intermediate, ranging between **1 nanometer and 1000 nanometers**. These particles do not settle upon standing but still exhibit the **Tyndall Effect**. *Hence, statement D is incorrect.*
 
• **Common Examples**: Typical examples of **suspensions** include **muddy water**, **chalk powder in water**, **flour in water**, and **Milk of Magnesia** (Magnesium Hydroxide).
 
• **Applications**: **Suspensions** are widely used in the **pharmaceutical industry**, where many **medicines** (like **antibiotics** or **antacids**) are prepared as **suspensions** to ensure the stability of the active ingredient before consumption.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Brownian Motion**: In **suspensions**, **Brownian motion** (the random movement of particles) is usually not strong enough to counteract **gravity**, leading to the eventual **sedimentation** of the particles.
 
• **Stokes' Law**: The rate at which particles in a **suspension** settle can be calculated using **Stokes' Law**, which depends on the **radius** of the particle, the **viscosity** of the medium, and the **density** difference.
 
• **Appearance**: **Suspensions** are generally **opaque** or **cloudy** because the large particles block or scatter **light waves** significantly.
 
• **Phase separation**: In a **suspension**, the two phases are often referred to as the **dispersed phase** (the solid particles) and the **dispersion medium** (the liquid or gas).

questions.question: Leucoplasts have which of the following colours?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**White**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Leucoplasts** are a category of **plastids** that are characterized by their lack of **pigments**. Because they do not contain any **colored pigments** like **chlorophyll** or **carotenoids**, they appear **white** or **colorless**.
 
• These organelles are primarily found in **non-photosynthetic** tissues of plants, such as **roots**, **bulbs**, **tubers**, and **seeds**, where light does not reach.
 
• The primary **function** of **leucoplasts** is the **storage** of **organic nutrients**. They act as **storage depots** for **starch**, **lipids**, and **proteins**.
 
• The term **leucoplast** was coined by **A. F. W. Schimper** in **1883**. He categorized **plastids** based on their **color** and **function**.
 
• Indigo is not the color associated with these organelles; **indigo** and **purple** hues in plants are usually derived from **anthocyanins** found in **vacuoles**, not **plastids**. ***Hence, statement A is incorrect.***
 
• **Orange** is a color typically associated with **chromoplasts**, which contain **carotenoid** pigments like **beta-carotene**. ***Hence, statement B is incorrect.***
 
• **Purple** color in plant parts like **petals** or **fruits** is typically due to water-soluble **pigments** and is not the natural state of a **leucoplast**. ***Hence, statement C is incorrect.***
 
• Since **leucoplasts** are **pigment-less** and appear **colorless** or **white** in plant tissues like the **flesh of a potato**. ***Hence, statement D is correct.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Classification of Leucoplasts:**

 
 
• **Amyloplasts**: These are the most common type of **leucoplast**. They are specialized for the **synthesis** and **storage** of **starch** granules. A classic **example** is the **potato tuber**, where **amyloplasts** are found in high **density**.
 
• **Elaioplasts** (or **Oleoplasts**): These are responsible for the **storage** of **fats**, **lipids**, and **oils**. They are frequently found in **seeds** (like **oilseeds**) and **liverworts**.
 
• **Proteinoplasts** (or **Aleuroplasts**): These **leucoplasts** store **proteins** and are typically found in **seeds**, specifically in the **aleurone layer** of **maize** or **pulses**.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with other Plastids:**
 
 
• **Chloroplasts**: These contain **chlorophyll a** and **chlorophyll b**. They are **green** in color and are the site of **photosynthesis** in **leaves**.
 
• **Chromoplasts**: These contain **fat-soluble** pigments like **carotene** and **xanthophylls**. They provide **yellow**, **orange**, or **red** colors to **flowers** and **ripening fruits** to attract **pollinators** and **dispersers**.
 
• **Gerontoplasts**: These are **plastids** that develop from **chloroplasts** during the **senescence** (aging) of plant **tissues**.
 
 
 
• **Interconvertibility:** It is a **fact** that **plastids** are **interconvertible**. For example, **leucoplasts** in a **potato** can turn into **chloroplasts** (green) if exposed to **sunlight** for a prolonged period, and **chloroplasts** turn into **chromoplasts** during the **ripening** of a **tomato**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Structure**: Like **mitochondria** and **chloroplasts**, **leucoplasts** are **double-membrane** bound organelles. They possess their own **DNA** (**ptDNA**) and **70S ribosomes**, making them **semi-autonomous**.
 
• **Evolutionary Origin**: According to the **Endosymbiotic Theory**, **plastids** originated from **cyanobacteria** that were engulfed by a **eukaryotic** cell approximately **1.5 billion years** ago.
 
• **Applications**: In **agricultural science**, the study of **amyloplasts** is crucial for understanding **crop yield** and **starch quality** in **staple foods** like **rice**, **wheat**, and **corn**.
 
• **Location**: While **chloroplasts** dominate the **mesophyll cells** of **leaves**, **leucoplasts** dominate the **parenchyma cells** of **storage organs**.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions will most effectively accelerate the corrosion of iron?

options.text: Iron surface exposed to moist air containing dissolved salts
Iron immersed in pure water, free of dissolved oxygen
Iron coated with a thin layer of zinc (galvanization)
Iron surface in dry air with no impurities

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Iron surface exposed to moist air containing dissolved salts**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Corrosion** is a natural process that converts a refined metal into a more stable oxide, hydroxide, or sulfide. In the case of **Iron**, this process is specifically called **rusting**, which requires both **oxygen** and **water**.
 
• An **iron surface exposed to moist air containing dissolved salts** provides the ideal environment for an **electrochemical cell** to form. The **dissolved salts** (like **Sodium Chloride** or **Magnesium Chloride**) act as an **electrolyte**, increasing the conductivity of the water film on the metal surface. This facilitates faster movement of ions and electrons, which significantly **accelerates the rate of corrosion**. *Hence, this condition is the most effective at accelerating the process.*
 
• If iron is **immersed in pure water free of dissolved oxygen**, the **oxidation** of iron cannot be sustained. Oxygen acts as the **oxidizing agent** at the **cathode** in the rusting reaction. Without it, the chemical cycle is broken. *Hence, this statement describes a condition that inhibits rather than accelerates corrosion.*
 
• **Galvanization** is a method of protection where iron is **coated with a thin layer of zinc**. Since **Zinc** is more **electropositive** and reactive than iron (higher in the **electrochemical series**), it undergoes **sacrificial corrosion** to protect the underlying iron. *Hence, this statement is incorrect as it refers to a prevention technique.*
 
• An **iron surface in dry air** lacks the necessary **moisture (H2O)** to form the aqueous medium required for ion transport. Corrosion is virtually non-existent in environments with **humidity** levels below **40%**. *Hence, this statement is incorrect regarding the acceleration of corrosion.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Chemical Formula of Rust**: The red-brown flaky substance formed is **hydrated iron(III) oxide**, represented by the chemical formula **Fe2O3·xH2O**.
 
• **The Redox Process**:
 
 
• At the **Anode**: Iron atoms lose electrons to form ferrous ions (**Fe → Fe2+ + 2e-**).
 
• At the **Cathode**: Oxygen and water accept these electrons to form hydroxide ions or water depending on the **pH** of the environment.
 
 
 
• **Factors Affecting Corrosion Rate**:
 
 
• **Presence of Impurities**: Pure metals corrode much slower than impure ones. Impurities act as tiny **cathodic sites**.
 
• **Air Pollution**: The presence of **Sulfur Dioxide (SO2)**, **Carbon Dioxide (CO2)**, and **Nitrogen Oxides (NOx)** in the atmosphere creates **acidic conditions** that dissolve protective oxide layers and speed up metal decay.
 
• **Temperature**: A rise in **temperature** generally increases the rate of chemical reactions, including the kinetic movement of ions in the electrolyte.
 
 
 
• **Methods of Prevention**:
 
 
• **Alloying**: Mixing iron with **Chromium** and **Nickel** produces **Stainless Steel**, which forms a **passive layer** of chromium oxide that prevents further oxidation.
 
• **Cathodic Protection**: Attaching a **sacrificial anode** made of **Magnesium** or **Zinc** to ships or underground pipes to ensure the iron remains the **cathode** and stays protected.
 
• **Barrier Protection**: Using **paints**, **grease**, or **plastic coatings** to physically block air and moisture.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Geographic Impact**: Corrosion is a major economic concern in **coastal areas**. Cities like **Mumbai** or **Kolkata** face higher infrastructure maintenance costs compared to inland cities due to the high **salinity** and **humidity** in the atmosphere.
 
• **Electrochemical Series**: Metals are ranked based on their **reduction potential**. Metals with a lower reduction potential (like **Zinc** and **Aluminium**) are more likely to corrode than metals with a higher potential (like **Gold** and **Silver**).
 
• **Economic Data**: According to various global **surveys**, the **annual cost of corrosion** is estimated to be approximately **3% to 4%** of a nation's **Gross Domestic Product (GDP)**, emphasizing the need for effective prevention technologies.

questions.question: The importance of genetic variation in organisms is that _________.

options.text: it leads to uniformity in the progeny
it gives rise to dominant and recessive traits
it increases the chances of survival of an organism

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**it increases the chances of survival of an organism**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Genetic variation** refers to the differences in **DNA sequences** among individuals within a **population**. It is the foundation of **evolution** and **natural selection**, providing the raw material upon which environmental pressures act.
 
• The primary importance of **genetic variation** is that it **increases the chances of survival** of a species. If an environment changes—due to **climate change**, the introduction of a new **pathogen**, or shifts in **food availability**—individuals with specific variations may possess traits that allow them to survive while others perish. *Hence, the statement in option D is correct.*
 
• **Genetic variation** prevents **uniformity**. **Uniformity in progeny** is typically a result of **asexual reproduction** or **cloning**, where offspring are genetically identical to the parent. While efficient, it makes the entire population susceptible to the same threats. *Hence, the statement in option A is incorrect.*
 
• While **sexual reproduction** is a significant mechanism that generates variation through **meiosis** and **random fertilization**, the "importance" of variation itself is the resulting **adaptability** and **survival**, rather than just the act of reproduction. *Hence, the statement in option B is incorrect.*
 
• **Dominant and recessive traits** are components of **Mendelian inheritance** and describe how certain **alleles** are expressed. While they contribute to the observable **phenotype**, they are a mechanism of variation rather than the ultimate reason why variation is biologically essential for a species' longevity. *Hence, the statement in option C is incorrect.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Sources of Variation:**

 
 
• **Mutation:** A permanent change in the **nucleotide sequence** of the **genome**. It is the ultimate source of new **alleles**. Mutations can be caused by **UV radiation**, **chemical mutagens**, or errors during **DNA replication**.
 
• **Gene Flow:** The transfer of **genetic material** between different **populations**. This occurs when individuals migrate and breed in a new location, introducing new **genes** into the local **gene pool**.
 
• **Sexual Reproduction:** During **prophase I** of **meiosis**, **crossing over** occurs between **homologous chromosomes**, creating unique combinations of **genes**.
 
 
 
• **Natural Selection:**
 
 
• Proposed by **Charles Darwin** in his **1859** book "On the Origin of Species." It describes the process where organisms better **adapted** to their environment tend to survive and produce more offspring.
 
• Without **genetic variation**, **natural selection** would have no "choices" to make, and **evolution** would cease.
 
 
 
• **Population Bottleneck:**
 
 
• A sharp reduction in the size of a **population** due to environmental events (like **earthquakes** or **floods**) or human activities. This reduces **genetic variation** and can lead to **inbreeding depression**, lowering the **survival rate** of the species.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Example of Variation (Peppered Moth):** In **19th-century England**, the **Biston betularia** (peppered moth) population shifted from light-colored to dark-colored due to **industrial pollution**. The **genetic variation** for wing color allowed the species to survive as the environment changed.
 
• **Antibiotic Resistance:** In **microbiology**, **genetic variation** in **bacteria** (often through **plasmids**) allows certain individuals to survive **antibiotic** treatment. These survivors multiply, leading to the **evolution** of resistant strains, a major challenge in modern **healthcare**.
 
• **Adaptation vs. Variation:** While **variation** refers to the differences present at a specific time, **adaptation** is the biological process where a population becomes better suited to its habitat over many **generations**.
 
• **Conservation Biology:** Scientists use **genetic diversity indices** to measure the health of **endangered species**. Low **variation** is often a precursor to **extinction**.

questions.question: Which of the following hydrocarbons is saturated?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Butane**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Saturated hydrocarbons** are organic compounds consisting entirely of **carbon** and **hydrogen** atoms where all the carbon-carbon bonds are **single bonds**. These are also known as **Alkanes**.
 
• **Butane** is a **saturated hydrocarbon** with the chemical formula **C4H10**. It follows the general formula for alkanes, which is **CnH2n+2**, where **n=4**. Since it contains only single bonds between its **four carbon atoms**, it is classified as saturated. ***Hence, Option D is correct.***
 
• The structure of **Butane** can be **linear (n-butane)** or **branched (isobutane)**, both of which are saturated because every carbon atom is bonded to the maximum possible number of hydrogen atoms.
 
• **Butane** is a colorless, highly flammable **gas** at room temperature and atmospheric pressure. It is commonly used as a **fuel** for cigarette lighters and as a component in **Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG)**.
 
• In a saturated hydrocarbon, every **carbon atom** is **sp3 hybridized**, meaning it forms **four sigma bonds** in a **tetrahedral geometry**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Butene (Option A):**

 
 
• **Butene** is an **unsaturated hydrocarbon** with the formula **C4H8**. It belongs to the **Alkene** series.
 
• It contains at least one **double bond** between carbon atoms, which means it has fewer hydrogen atoms than the corresponding alkane (butane). ***Hence, Option A is incorrect.***
 
• It is primarily used in the production of **polymers** and **synthetic rubber** in the **petrochemical industry**.
 
 
 
• **Benzene (Option B):**
 
 
• **Benzene** is an **aromatic hydrocarbon** with the molecular formula **C6H6**.
 
• It consists of **six carbon atoms** joined in a ring with **delocalized pi electrons**, often represented as alternating **double bonds**. This structure makes it highly **unsaturated**. ***Hence, Option B is incorrect.***
 
• It is a natural constituent of **crude oil** and is a vital industrial chemical used to make **plastics, resins, nylon, and synthetic fibers**.
 
 
 
• **Propene (Option C):**
 
 
• **Propene**, also known as **propylene**, is an **unsaturated hydrocarbon** with the formula **C3H6**.
 
• As an **alkene**, it contains one **carbon-carbon double bond**. ***Hence, Option C is incorrect.***
 
• It is the **second simplest** member of the alkene class and is a major raw material for the production of **polypropylene** plastic.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Chemical Reactivity:** **Saturated hydrocarbons** (alkanes) are generally **less reactive** than unsaturated ones because single **C-C** and **C-H** bonds are very strong. They typically undergo **substitution reactions** (like halogenation) rather than addition reactions.
 
• **Unsaturated Hydrocarbons:** These include **Alkenes** (double bonds) and **Alkynes** (triple bonds). They are more **reactive** because the double or triple bonds can "open up" to bond with other atoms in **addition reactions**.
 
• **Identification:** A common test to distinguish between saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons is the **Bromine Water Test**. **Unsaturated** hydrocarbons will **decolorize** reddish-brown bromine water, while **saturated** hydrocarbons like **Butane** will not react with it under normal conditions.
 
• **Isomerism:** While **Butane** has **two isomers** (n-butane and isobutane), **Propene** and **Butene** exhibit different types of isomerism, including **positional** and **geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism** due to the presence of the **double bond**.

questions.question: What is corrosion most commonly observed as?

options.text: Boiling of water in a kettle

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Rust formation on iron objects**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Corrosion** is a natural process that converts a refined **metal** into a more chemically stable form such as **oxide**, **hydroxide**, or **sulfide**. It is the gradual destruction of materials by chemical and/or electrochemical reaction with their environment.
 
• **Rusting** is the most common form of corrosion observed in daily life, specifically occurring on **iron** and its **alloys** like **steel**. It occurs when **iron** reacts with **oxygen** and **moisture** (water) in the air to form **hydrated ferric oxide**. ***Hence, the statement regarding rust formation is correct.***
 
• The chemical formula for **rust** is **Fe2O3·nH2O**. This reddish-brown flaky substance weakens the **structural integrity** of the **metal**, leading to significant **economic loss** and safety hazards in **bridges**, **buildings**, and **vehicles**.
 
• **Glowing of a bulb** is a physical process where the **filament** (usually **tungsten**) gets heated to a high temperature and emits **light**. It does not involve the chemical degradation of the metal in the way corrosion does. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***
 
• **Boiling of water** is a **physical change** or phase transition from **liquid** to **gas** occurring at **100 degrees Celsius** (at standard pressure). It is not related to the chemical corrosion of metals. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***
 
• **Melting of metal** is also a **physical change** where a solid metal turns into a **liquid** state upon reaching its **melting point**. While high temperatures can accelerate corrosion, melting itself is not corrosion. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Types of Corrosion in Other Metals:**

 
 
• **Silver Tarnish:** When **silver** objects are exposed to air containing **hydrogen sulfide**, they develop a black coating of **silver sulfide (Ag2S)**.
 
• **Copper Verdigris:** **Copper** reacts with moist **carbon dioxide** in the air to slowly lose its shiny brown surface and gain a green coat of **basic copper carbonate**.
 
• **Aluminium Passivation:** Unlike iron, **aluminium** forms a very thin, tough layer of **aluminium oxide** that actually protects the rest of the metal from further corrosion.
 
 
 
• **Factors Influencing Corrosion:**
 
 
• **Moisture:** The presence of **water** or **humidity** is essential for the electrochemical process of **rusting**.
 
• **Salinity:** **Saltwater** (electrolytes) significantly speeds up the rate of **corrosion**, which is why ships and coastal structures deteriorate faster.
 
• **pH Levels:** Exposure to **acid rain** or acidic environments increases the **oxidation** rate of metals.
 
 
 
• **Prevention Methods:**
 
 
• **Galvanization:** Coating **iron** or **steel** with a thin layer of **zinc**. Even if the coating is scratched, **zinc** corrodes preferentially (sacrificial protection).
 
• **Electroplating:** Using **electricity** to coat a metal with a layer of another metal like **chromium** or **tin** to prevent **oxidation**.
 
• **Alloying:** Mixing metals with other elements. For example, **Stainless Steel** is an alloy of **iron**, **chromium**, and **nickel** that does not rust easily.
 
• **Painting and Greasing:** Applying a barrier of **paint**, **oil**, or **grease** to prevent the metal surface from coming into contact with **air** and **moisture**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Redox Reaction:** Corrosion is essentially a **redox** (reduction-oxidation) reaction. In **iron**, the metal acts as an **anode** and is **oxidized** to **Fe2+** ions, while **oxygen** is **reduced** at the **cathode**.
 
• **Economic Impact:** According to various global **surveys**, the **annual cost** of corrosion is estimated to be over **3%** of the global **GDP**, highlighting the importance of **anti-corrosion** technologies.
 
• **Microbial Corrosion:** Some types of corrosion are caused by **bacteria** (Sulphate-reducing bacteria) that can thrive in **pipelines** and **underground tanks**, leading to rapid **pitting** and failure.

questions.question: Which of the following devices does NOT use the heating effect of current for its working?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Electric Mixer Grinder**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **heating effect of electric current**, also known as **Joule heating**, occurs when an electric current passes through a conductor with **resistance**, leading to the production of **heat energy**.
 
• **Electric Mixer Grinder**: This device primarily works on the **magnetic effect of electric current**. It contains an **electric motor** that converts **electrical energy** into **mechanical energy** to rotate the blades. While it may get warm due to friction and internal resistance, its primary working principle is not the heating effect. ***Hence, statement A is correct.***
 
• **Electric Iron**: This appliance uses a **heating element** made of high-resistance material like **Nichrome**. When current flows through it, the resistance converts the **electrical energy** into **heat**, which is then used to press clothes. ***Hence, statement B is incorrect.***
 
• **Electric Geyser**: It functions by passing current through an **immersion rod** or a heating coil. The high **resistance** of the coil generates significant **thermal energy**, which is transferred to the **water** to increase its **temperature**. ***Hence, statement C is incorrect.***
 
• **Electric Fuse**: A **fuse** is a critical safety device designed to protect circuits. It consists of a **wire** with a **low melting point**. When **excessive current** flows, the **heating effect** causes the wire to **melt** and break the **circuit**. ***Hence, statement D is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Joule’s Law of Heating**: The amount of heat produced (**H**) in a conductor is directly proportional to the **square of the current** (**I²**), the **resistance** (**R**) of the conductor, and the **time** (**t**) for which the current flows. The formula is expressed as **H = I²Rt**.
 
• **Magnetic Effect of Current**: Discovered by **Hans Christian Oersted** in **1820**, this principle states that a **current-carrying conductor** produces a **magnetic field** around it. This is the fundamental principle behind **electric motors**, **fans**, and **mixers**.
 
• **Nichrome**: It is an **alloy** consisting of **Nickel** and **Chromium**. It is widely used in heating appliances because of its **high resistivity** and high **melting point**, and because it does not **oxidize** (burn) easily at **high temperatures**.
 
• **Energy Transformation**: In heating devices, **electrical energy** is transformed into **heat energy**. In motorized devices like the **Mixer Grinder**, **electrical energy** is transformed into **kinetic energy** (mechanical energy).
 
• **Applications of Heating Effect**: Apart from irons and geysers, other examples include **electric toasters**, **electric kettles**, **room heaters**, and **hair dryers**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Resistance Factor**: The **efficiency** of a heating device depends on the **material** used. For example, **Copper** has low resistance and is used for **connecting wires** to prevent heat loss, while **Tungsten** is used in **bulbs** because it can withstand **temperatures** up to **3422 degrees Celsius** while emitting **light**.
 
• **Fuse Characteristics**: A **fuse wire** is typically made of an **alloy of tin and lead**. It must have **high resistance** (to heat up quickly) and a **low melting point** (to break the circuit promptly during a **short circuit** or **overload**).
 
• **Safety in Appliances**: Modern homes often use **MCBs (Miniature Circuit Breakers)** instead of traditional fuses. While fuses work on the **heating effect**, **MCBs** often utilize the **magnetic effect** to trip the switch during **faults**.

questions.question: What is the correct definition of atomic mass?

options.text: It is the mass of an atom in grams.
It is the mass of one atom in kilograms.
It is the mass relative to carbon-12 atom.
It is the mass of one hydrogen molecule.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It is the mass relative to carbon-12 atom**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Atomic mass** is the mass of a single atom, which includes the mass of **protons**, **neutrons**, and **electrons**. However, because the mass of an atom is extremely small, it is expressed as a relative value rather than an absolute mass in standard SI units like grams or kilograms.
 
• The modern standard for atomic mass is based on the **carbon-12** isotope. By international agreement in **1961**, the **International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC)** defined one **atomic mass unit (amu)** as exactly **1/12th** of the mass of one atom of **carbon-12**.
 
• Defining atomic mass as the **mass relative to carbon-12 atom** allows scientists to create a stable scale where the mass of **hydrogen** is approximately **1** and **oxygen** is approximately **16**. *Hence, statement C is correct.*
 
• While an atom does have a mass that can be measured in **grams**, the value is so tiny (approximately **10^-24 grams**) that it is not used as the standard definition in chemical equations or the **periodic table**. *Hence, statement A is incorrect.*
 
• Similarly, **kilograms** are the standard **SI unit** for mass, but they are inconvenient for describing individual atomic particles without using massive negative exponents. *Hence, statement B is incorrect.*
 
• **Hydrogen** was the original reference point for **John Dalton** in the **19th century**, but it was replaced first by **oxygen** and later by **carbon-12** for greater precision in **mass spectrometry**. *Hence, statement D is incorrect.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Unified Atomic Mass Unit (u):** This unit, also known as the **Dalton (Da)**, is used to express atomic and molecular weights. **1 u** is approximately equal to **1.660539 x 10^-27 kilograms**.
 
• **Average Atomic Mass:** Most elements found in nature are a mixture of several **isotopes** (atoms of the same element with different numbers of **neutrons**). The atomic mass listed on the **Periodic Table** is the **weighted average** of all naturally occurring isotopes of that element.
 
• **Mass Number vs. Atomic Mass:** The **mass number** is a whole number representing the sum of **protons** and **neutrons** in a nucleus. In contrast, the **atomic mass** is a more precise decimal value that accounts for the **binding energy** and the small mass contribution of **electrons**.
 
• **Avogadro’s Number:** There is a crucial relationship between atomic mass units and grams. **One mole** of an element has a mass in **grams** that is numerically equal to its **atomic mass** in **u**. This is governed by **Avogadro's constant** (**6.022 x 10^23**).
 
• **Applications:** Understanding atomic mass is fundamental in **Stoichiometry**, **Molecular Biology**, and **Nuclear Physics** to calculate the amount of reactants needed in **chemical reactions** or to determine the **molecular formula** of unknown substances.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Isotopes of Carbon:** While **Carbon-12** is the standard, **Carbon-13** and **Carbon-14** also exist. **Carbon-12** was chosen because it is the most abundant and stable, making it a reliable reference for **analytical chemistry**.
 
• **History of Standards:** Before **1961**, physicists used **oxygen-16** while chemists used a natural mixture of **oxygen isotopes** as a standard. The move to **carbon-12** unified these two scales into a single **International Scale of Atomic Weights**.

questions.question: A sound of 100 { Hz} is compared with a sound of 500 { Hz} . Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: 100 Hz sound has a higher pitch.
500 Hz sound has a higher pitch.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**500 Hz sound has a higher pitch**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Pitch** is a sensory characteristic of sound that allows a listener to assign it a position on a musical scale based on its **frequency**. It determines how "shrill" or "grave" a sound appears to the human ear.
 
• The **frequency** of a sound wave is defined as the number of **vibrations** or cycles completed per unit of time, specifically per **second**. The standard unit for measuring frequency is **Hertz (Hz)**.
 
• There is a direct proportional relationship between frequency and pitch: a sound with a **higher frequency** will always have a **higher pitch**, while a sound with a **lower frequency** will have a **lower pitch**.
 
• In the given comparison, the sound of **500 Hz** completes **500 cycles per second**, whereas the sound of **100 Hz** completes only **100 cycles per second**. Therefore, the **500 Hz** sound is much more shrill. ***Hence, the statement "500 Hz sound has a higher pitch" is correct.***
 
• The statement that both have the same pitch is false because pitch is strictly dependent on frequency, and these two frequencies are different. ***Hence, the statement "Both have the same pitch" is incorrect.***
 
• The statement claiming the 100 Hz sound is higher is physically impossible under standard acoustic laws because **100 Hz** is a lower frequency than **500 Hz**. ***Hence, the statement "100 Hz sound has a higher pitch" is incorrect.***
 
• Since pitch is a measurable and quantifiable property related to frequency, it can easily be compared using objective data. ***Hence, the statement "Pitch cannot be compared" is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Human Audibility Range**: The standard range of **audible frequencies** for a healthy human ear is between **20 Hz** and **20,000 Hz** (or **20 kHz**). Frequency values outside this range are generally not perceived as sound by humans.
 
• **Infrasonic and Ultrasonic**: Sounds with a frequency lower than **20 Hz** are categorized as **infrasonic** (e.g., sounds produced by elephants or earthquakes). Sounds with a frequency higher than **20,000 Hz** are **ultrasonic** (e.g., sounds used by bats for navigation or in medical **ultrasound** imaging).
 
• **Loudness vs. Pitch**: It is crucial to distinguish pitch from **loudness**. **Pitch** depends on **frequency**, whereas **loudness** depends on the **amplitude** (the maximum displacement of the particles of the medium). A sound can be high-pitched but very quiet, or low-pitched and very loud.
 
• **Wavelength Relationship**: Frequency and **wavelength** are inversely proportional. This means a high-pitched **500 Hz** sound has a **shorter wavelength**, while a low-pitched **100 Hz** sound has a **longer wavelength**, assuming they travel through the same medium like **air** at a constant **temperature**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Biological Factors**: In humans, the pitch of the voice is determined by the **vocal cords**. **Women** and **children** typically have shorter and thinner vocal cords that vibrate faster, producing a **higher frequency** and thus a **higher pitch** voice compared to adult **men**.
 
• **Speed of Sound**: The **speed of sound** in a specific medium (such as dry air at **20 degrees Celsius**, where it is approximately **343 meters per second**) is independent of the frequency. Therefore, both the **100 Hz** and **500 Hz** sounds travel at the **same speed** in the same environment.
 
• **Musical Octaves**: In music, an **octave** is the interval between one musical pitch and another with double its frequency. For example, a note at **500 Hz** is approximately one octave higher than a note at **250 Hz**.

questions.question: A body of mass 5 { kg} is moving with an acceleration of 2 { m/s}² . What is the force acting on it?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**10 N**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• According to **Newton's Second Law of Motion**, the **force** acting on an object is directly proportional to the product of its **mass** and **acceleration**. This fundamental principle of **Classical Mechanics** provides the quantitative description of force.
 
• The mathematical expression for this law is **F = m x a**, where **F** is the **net force**, **m** is the **mass** of the body, and **a** is the **acceleration** produced.
 
• In the provided problem, the **mass (m)** of the body is given as **5 kg** and the **acceleration (a)** is **2 m/s2**.
 
• By applying the formula, the **Force (F)** is calculated as **5 kg multiplied by 2 m/s2**, which equals **10 kg.m/s2** or **10 N**. ***Hence, the statement regarding the force being 10 N is correct.***
 
• The unit of **force** in the **International System of Units (SI)** is the **Newton**, symbolized by **N**. One **Newton** is defined as the **amount of force** required to provide an **acceleration** of **1 m/s2** to a **mass** of **1 kg**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Newton's Laws of Motion:**

 
 
• **Sir Isaac Newton** first presented these **three laws** in his work **Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica**, published in the **year 1687**.
 
• **First Law (Law of Inertia):** An object will remain at **rest** or move in a **straight line** at a **constant velocity** unless acted upon by an **external force**.
 
• **Third Law (Action and Reaction):** For every **action force**, there is an **equal and opposite reaction force** acting on two different bodies.
 
 
 
• **Vector Nature of Force:**
 
 
• **Force** is a **vector quantity**, meaning it possesses both **magnitude** and **direction**.
 
• In this calculation, the **magnitude** is **10 N**, and the **direction** of the force would be the same as the **direction** of the **acceleration**.
 
 
 
• **Mass vs. Weight:**
 
 
• The **mass** of an object (measured in **kg**) is a measure of its **inertia** and remains **constant** regardless of **location**.
 
• The **weight** is the **gravitational force** acting on that **mass**, calculated as **W = m x g**, where **g** is approximately **9.8 m/s2** on **Earth**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **SI Unit Conversion:** The **Newton (N)** can be broken down into **base units** as **kg.m.s-2**. In the **CGS system**, the unit of **force** is the **dyne**, where **1 Newton** is equal to **100,000 (10⁵) dynes**.
 
• **Concept of Net Force:** The **Newton's Second Law** specifically refers to the **net force** (the **vector sum** of all **individual forces**) acting on the body. If multiple **forces** act in **opposite directions**, they must be **subtracted** to find the **resultant force**.
 
• **Applications:** This principle is used in **engineering**, **aerospace**, and **automotive safety** (such as calculating the **impact force** during a **collision** at a specific **deceleration**).
 
• **Relationship:** If the **mass** is doubled while keeping the **acceleration** constant, the **force** required will **double**. Conversely, if **mass** is constant and **acceleration** is doubled, the **force** also **doubles**, showing a **linear relationship**.

questions.question: Which component of phloem is basically responsible for the translocation of food?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sieve elements**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Sieve elements** are the specialized cells in the **phloem** tissue that are primarily responsible for the **translocation of food** (organic solutes like **sucrose**) from the leaves (source) to other parts of the plant (sink). ***Hence, statement B is correct.***
 
• In **angiosperms**, these elements are known as **sieve tube members**, which join end-to-end to form continuous **sieve tubes**. Their end walls, called **sieve plates**, have pores that allow the flow of sap between cells.
 
• **Phloem parenchyma** consists of living cells that mainly function in the **storage of food**, resins, latex, and mucilage, and contribute to the **lateral conduction** of food rather than primary long-distance translocation. ***Hence, statement A is incorrect.***
 
• **Phloem fibres**, also known as **bast fibres**, are **sclerenchymatous cells** that provide **mechanical support** and strength to the plant; they are generally **dead at maturity** and do not participate in food transport. ***Hence, statement C is incorrect.***
 
• **Companion cells** are specialized **parenchymatous cells** closely associated with sieve tube elements; while they help in **loading and unloading of sugars** into the sieve tubes using **ATP**, they are not the actual channels through which food is translocated. ***Hence, statement D is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Phloem** is a **complex permanent tissue** in vascular plants. It was named by **Carl Nageli** in **1858**, derived from the Greek word "phloios," meaning bark.
 
• Unlike **xylem**, which conducts water and minerals primarily **unidirectionally** (upwards), phloem transport is **bidirectional**, moving nutrients both up and down the plant stem.
 
• The process of food transport in phloem is called **translocation**, which is explained by the **Mass Flow Hypothesis** (or Pressure Flow Hypothesis) proposed by **Ernst Munch** in **1930**.
 
• **Sieve tube elements** are unique because they are **living cells** but **lack a nucleus**, ribosomes, and vacuoles at maturity to provide more space for the efficient flow of nutrients.
 
• In **gymnosperms** and lower vascular plants, the food-conducting elements are **sieve cells**, which are less specialized than the sieve tube members found in flowering plants.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Companion cells** and sieve tube members are called **"sister cells"** because they originate from the same **meristematic mother cell** through a single longitudinal division.
 
• The **phloem sap** is mainly composed of **water and sucrose**, but it also transports **amino acids**, **hormones**, and other minerals throughout the plant body.
 
• Among the four components of phloem, **phloem fibres** are the only **dead cells**, while sieve tubes, companion cells, and phloem parenchyma are **living cells**.
 
• **Economic Use:** Phloem fibres of certain plants like **Jute, Flax, and Hemp** are used commercially to make ropes, textiles, and bags due to their high **mechanical strength**.
 
• The **sieve pores** are often lined with a carbohydrate called **callose**, which can block the pores in response to injury or seasonal changes to prevent the loss of precious sap.

questions.question: Hormone named testosterone is secreted from which of the following parts of a human being?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Testis**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Testosterone** is the primary **male sex hormone** and is also considered an **anabolic steroid**. It plays a crucial role in the development of **male reproductive tissues** such as the **testis** and **prostate**.
 
• In **human beings**, particularly males, **testosterone** is primarily secreted by the **Leydig cells** (also known as **interstitial cells**) located within the **testes**. Approximately **95%** of the testosterone in a male body is produced in the **testes**.
 
• The secretion of this hormone is strictly regulated by the **Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal axis**. The **Anterior Pituitary gland** releases **Luteinizing Hormone (LH)**, which travels through the bloodstream to the **testes** to stimulate the production of **testosterone**.
 
• Its primary **functions** include promoting **secondary sexual characteristics** during **puberty** (typically starting between the **ages** of **9 and 14**), such as the growth of **body hair**, deepening of the **voice**, and increase in **muscle mass** and **bone density**.
 
• While **testosterone** is the principal **androgen** in males, it is also present in **females** in much smaller quantities, produced by the **ovaries** and the **adrenal glands**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Fallopian tube**: These are the **uterine tubes** in the **female reproductive system** that transport the **ovum** from the **ovary** to the **uterus** each month. They are the site where **fertilization** usually occurs; however, they do not secrete **testosterone**. Hence, this option is **incorrect**.
 
• **Ureter**: The **ureter** is a muscular tube that carries **urine** from the **kidneys** to the **urinary bladder**. There are **two ureters** in the human body, one attached to each **kidney**. It is an organ of the **urinary system** and has no endocrine function related to **sex hormones**. Hence, this option is **incorrect**.
 
• **Testis**: The **testes** (plural) are the male **gonads** located inside the **scrotum**. They are responsible for **spermatogenesis** (production of **sperm**) and the endocrine function of producing **androgens** like **testosterone**. Hence, this option is **correct**.
 
• **Uterus**: The **uterus**, or **womb**, is a hollow muscular organ located in the **female pelvis** between the **bladder** and **rectum**. Its primary **function** is to nourish the **developing fetus** prior to birth. It does not produce **testosterone**. Hence, this option is **incorrect**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Normal Levels**: In adult **men**, normal **testosterone** levels generally range from **300 to 1,000 nanograms per deciliter (ng/dL)**. Levels tend to peak around **age 20** and gradually decline after **age 30**.
 
• **Chemical Nature**: **Testosterone** is derived from **cholesterol**. It acts through **androgen receptors** found in various tissues throughout the body to exert its **genomic effects**.
 
• **Discovery**: The hormone was first isolated and synthesized in the **year 1935** by researchers **Karoly David**, **Ernst Laqueur**, and colleagues.
 
• **Health Impact**: Low levels of **testosterone** (known as **hypogonadism**) can lead to symptoms such as **fatigue**, **depression**, reduced **libido**, and **osteoporosis**. Conversely, **synthetic testosterone** is often used in **hormone replacement therapy** and by **athletes** (often illegally) to enhance **performance** and **muscle growth**.

questions.question: A student places an object at a distance greater than twice the focal length from a convex lens. What kind of image is formed?

options.text: Virtual, erect, and smaller than the object
Virtual, erect, and larger than the object
Real, inverted, and larger than the object
Real, inverted, and smaller than the object

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Real, inverted, and smaller than the object**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• When an **object** is placed at a **distance greater than twice the focal length (2f)** from a **convex lens**, the light rays coming from the object undergo **refraction** and converge on the opposite side of the lens.
 
• The **image** is formed between the **focus (F2)** and the **center of curvature (2F2)** on the other side of the lens. ***Hence, the statement regarding the image being real and inverted is correct.***
 
• The nature of the image is **real** because the light rays actually intersect at a point after passing through the lens, meaning the image can be caught on a **screen**.
 
• The orientation of the image is **inverted** (upside down) relative to the object. ***Hence, the statement regarding the orientation is correct.***
 
• The size of the image produced is **diminished** or **smaller than the object** itself. This occurs because the rays converge closer to the principal axis than their point of origin. ***Hence, the final conclusion of the question is correct.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Convex Lens Characteristics:** A **convex lens**, also known as a **converging lens**, is thicker at the center than at the edges. It has a **positive focal length** according to the **Cartesian sign convention**. It is widely used in **optical instruments** such as **microscopes**, **telescopes**, and **cameras**.
 
• **Image Formation at Different Positions:**
 
 
• **At Infinity:** The image is formed at the **focus (F)**, is **real, inverted**, and **highly diminished** (point-sized).
 
• **At 2F:** The image is formed at **2F** on the other side, is **real, inverted**, and the **same size** as the object.
 
• **Between F and 2F:** The image is formed **beyond 2F**, is **real, inverted**, and **magnified** (larger than the object).
 
• **At F:** The image is formed at **infinity**, is **real, inverted**, and **highly magnified**.
 
• **Between F and Optical Center (O):** The image is **virtual, erect**, and **magnified**, formed on the **same side** as the object.
 
 
 
• **Applications in Vision:** Convex lenses are used to correct **Hypermetropia** (long-sightedness), where the person can see distant objects clearly but struggles with near objects. The lens helps in converging light rays so they focus correctly on the **retina**.
 
• **Magnifying Glass:** A simple **magnifying glass** is a convex lens used to view small objects by placing the object within the **focal length**, resulting in a **virtual, erect, and enlarged image**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Lens Formula:** The relationship between the **object distance (u)**, **image distance (v)**, and **focal length (f)** is given by the formula: **1/f = 1/v - 1/u**.
 
• **Magnification (m):** It is defined as the ratio of the **height of the image (hi)** to the **height of the object (ho)**, represented as **m = hi / ho = v / u**. For **real images**, the magnification is **negative**, and for **virtual images**, it is **positive**.
 
• **Power of a Lens:** The **power (P)** is the reciprocal of the **focal length** measured in **meters** (P = 1/f). The **SI unit** of power is the **Dioptre (D)**. A convex lens has **positive power**.
 
• **Refractive Index:** The degree of **convergence** depends on the **refractive index** of the lens material (usually **glass** or **plastic**) and the **curvature** of the lens surfaces.

questions.question: How does the Mimosa pudica (touch-me-not) plant transmit the touch stimulus from the point of contact to the motor cells responsible for movement?

options.text: Through growth of new supportive cells at the touch site
By releasing hormones that travel through specialised tubes
Through specialised nerve tissues connecting the points
Through electrical and chemical signals passed between general plant cells

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Through electrical and chemical signals passed between general plant cells**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The movement in **Mimosa pudica** (commonly known as the **touch-me-not** or **sensitive plant**) is a classic example of **seismonastic** or **thigmonastic movement**. This is a rapid, non-directional response to a physical stimulus like **touch**, **pressure**, or **heat**.
 
• Unlike animals, plants do not possess a **nervous system**, **nerve tissues**, or **muscles** to coordinate movement. Instead, they utilize **electrical and chemical signals** to transmit information from the point of contact to other parts of the plant. *Hence, statement D is correct.*
 
• The transmission does not involve the **growth of new cells**, as growth-related movements (like **tropisms**) are much slower and often irreversible, whereas the folding of **Mimosa** leaves happens in **seconds** and is reversible. *Hence, statement A is incorrect.*
 
• While plants do use **hormones** (like **auxins** or **ethylene**) for long-distance signaling, hormonal transport through **phloem** or **xylem** is too slow to account for the near-instantaneous folding observed in this plant. *Hence, statement B is incorrect.*
 
• Plants lack **specialized nerve tissues**; the electrical impulses, known as **action potentials**, travel through general plant cells and specialized vascular tissues like the **protoxylem** and **protophloem**. *Hence, statement C is incorrect.*
 
• The actual movement occurs in a specialized organ called the **pulvinus**, located at the base of the **petiole** and **leaflets**. When the signal reaches the **pulvinus**, it triggers a sudden change in **turgor pressure**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Mechanism of Turgor Change:** The **electrical signal** causes **potassium ions (K+)** and **chloride ions (Cl-)** to exit the **motor cells** in the **pulvinus**. This movement of ions is followed by **water** leaving the cells through **osmosis**, causing the cells to collapse and the leaves to fold.
 
• **Plant Profile:** **Mimosa pudica** belongs to the **Fabaceae** family. It is **native** to **South** and **Central America**, though it is now widely distributed in **tropical regions** globally, including **India** and **Southeast Asia**.
 
• **Biological Function:** This rapid movement is believed to be a **defense mechanism** against **herbivores**. By folding its leaves, the plant appears wilted or smaller, and it may expose sharp **thorns** on the stem to discourage animals from eating it.
 
• **Nastic vs. Tropic Movements:** **Nastic movements** (like the touch response) are **independent** of the direction of the stimulus, whereas **tropic movements** (like **phototropism**) are **growth-dependent** and occur in the **direction** of the stimulus (e.g., towards light).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Signal Velocity:** In **Mimosa pudica**, the electrical signal can travel at speeds ranging from **5 to 100 millimeters per second**, which is exceptionally fast for the plant kingdom.
 
• **Recovery Time:** After the stimulus is removed, the plant gradually pumps **ions** back into the **motor cells**, allowing **water** to re-enter and restore **turgor pressure**. This recovery process usually takes **10 to 30 minutes**.
 
• **Research Data:** Studies have shown that the plant can "learn" and habituate to repeated non-threatening stimuli, a phenomenon known as **behavioral plasticity**, which suggests a higher level of **environmental processing** than previously thought for non-neural organisms.

questions.question: The image formed by a convex mirror is always _________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**virtual and erect**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **convex mirror**, also known as a **diverging mirror**, is a curved mirror in which the reflective surface bulges toward the light source. It always forms an image that is **virtual**, **erect**, and **diminished** (smaller than the object), regardless of the distance between the object and the mirror.
 
• **Statement A (Real and erect)**: In optics, **real images** are typically formed by the actual convergence of light rays and are almost always **inverted**. A single mirror cannot produce an image that is simultaneously real and erect for a real object. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***
 
• **Statement B (Virtual and erect)**: For a **convex mirror**, light rays incident on the surface diverge after reflection. These rays appear to originate from a point behind the mirror. Since the rays do not actually meet, the image is **virtual** and stays **upright** or **erect**. ***Hence, this statement is correct.***
 
• **Statement C (Virtual and inverted)**: According to the principles of ray optics for spherical mirrors, **virtual images** are always **erect** with respect to the object. An inverted virtual image is not possible in this configuration. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***
 
• **Statement D (Real and inverted)**: This is a characteristic feature of a **concave mirror** when the object is placed at a distance greater than the **focal length**. A convex mirror lacks the ability to converge rays to a real point in front of the mirror. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***
 
• The position of the image in a **convex mirror** is always between the **pole (P)** and the **principal focus (F)**, located behind the mirror.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Field of View**: One of the most significant **features** of a **convex mirror** is its **wide field of view**. Because the mirror curves outwards, it allows the observer to see a much larger area compared to a **plane mirror** or a **concave mirror**.
 
• **Applications**: Due to the **virtual and erect** nature of the image and the wide coverage, these mirrors are extensively used as **rear-view mirrors** in **vehicles** (cars, bikes, trucks). They are also used as **security mirrors** in **shops**, **ATMs**, and at **blind turns** on roads to prevent accidents.
 
• **Mirror Formula**: The mathematical relationship for these mirrors is given by **1/v + 1/u = 1/f**, where **v** is the image distance, **u** is the object distance, and **f** is the **focal length**.
 
• **Sign Convention**: According to the **Cartesian sign convention**, the **focal length (f)** and the **radius of curvature (R)** of a **convex mirror** are always taken as **positive** because they lie behind the reflecting surface.
 
• **Magnification (m)**: The **magnification** produced by a **convex mirror** is always **positive** and **less than 1** (m 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Comparison with Concave Mirror**: Unlike a convex mirror, a **concave mirror** can form **real**, **inverted**, **virtual**, **erect**, **magnified**, or **diminished** images depending on the **location** of the object relative to the **center of curvature (C)** and **focus (F)**.
 
• **Nature of Rays**: In a convex mirror, parallel rays of light coming from **infinity** appear to diverge from the **principal focus** after reflection. This is why the focus is considered **virtual**.
 
• **Image Size**: As the object moves closer to the **pole** of a **convex mirror**, the **size** of the **virtual image** increases slightly but always remains **smaller than the actual object**.
 
• **Date and Discovery**: The mathematical properties of spherical mirrors were refined during the **17th century** with the advancement of **Euclidean geometry** and **optics** by scientists like **Ibn al-Haytham** and later **Johannes Kepler**.
